tasks.q: Press Run and watch the numbers come down.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
A while loop that never changes its variable runs for ever.
The site stops a runaway program after a few seconds. It is a normal mistake, not a disaster.
tasks.fb: Three parts: n is set before the loop, tested in the condition, and made smaller inside it.
tasks.starter:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
print("Lift off")

teach.say: A while loop repeats for as long as its condition stays true. It has three parts. Set the variable before the loop. Test it in the condition. Change it inside the loop. Miss out that last part and the condition never becomes false, so the loop never stops.

lines: Set n to 3 before the loop starts.
Keep going while n is above 0.
Show what n is holding.
Take 1 off n, so the condition gets closer to false.
This line is not indented, so it runs once, after the loop.

tasks.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: n reaches 4, the condition 4 < 4 is false, and the loop stops before 4 is ever displayed.

teach.say: A while loop can count upwards as well. The condition is tested before every turn, so the loop stops as soon as the condition is false.

tasks.q: Change the program so it displays the numbers `1` to `6`, one on each line.
brief: Change only the number in the condition.
Display the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, one on each line.
tasks.fb: The condition is where a while loop's finishing point lives.
tasks.starter:
n = 1
while n <= 3:
    print(n)
    n = n + 1

tests.why: The loop still stops at 3, so the number in the condition was not changed.

hint.think: The condition decides how far the loop goes before it stops.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it counts down from the number typed in to `1`, one number on each line.
brief: The first three lines are written for you.
The user types in one whole number, which is never less than `1`.
Replace ____ with one instruction of your own.
Display the numbers from the one typed down to `1`, one on each line.
tasks.fb: Set it, test it, change it. The third part is the one beginners leave out.
tasks.starter:
n = int(input())
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    ____

tests.why: Replace the ____ with an instruction that makes n smaller.
A 1 gives exactly one turn, because 0 is not above 0.
If this never finished, n was never changed inside the loop.

hint.think: The number has to get smaller on every turn, or the condition stays true for ever.
walk: The loop runs while n is above `0`.
Something inside the loop has to bring n closer to `0`.

teach.say: The line that changes the variable goes inside the loop, indented like the print. Without it the condition is tested on the same value every turn.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display every number from `1` up to that number, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than `1`.
The number typed in is displayed as well, on the last line.
Use a while loop, not a for loop.
tasks.fb: A while loop will count for you, but you have to set the counter up and move it on yourself.
tasks.starter: # Count up to the number typed in

tests.why: Nothing came out, so the counter was never displayed inside the loop.
A 1 gives one line. Nothing at all means the condition used < where <= was needed.
If this never finished, the counter was not changed inside the loop.

hint.think: You need a counter of your own, because a while loop does not make one for you.

teach.say: A counting while loop sets its counter before the loop, tests it against the finishing value, and adds 1 to it inside the loop.

lines: The finishing value, written into the program here.
Set the counter before the loop.
Keep going while the counter has not passed the finishing value.
Show the counter.
Add 1 to the counter, so the loop gets closer to stopping.
require: This one is for practising the while loop, so your program has to use one.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display every even number from `2` up to that number, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than `2`.
Start at `2` and go up in twos.
Display the number typed in as well, if it is even.
tasks.fb: The size of the step is yours to choose, and it is what decides which numbers the loop lands on.
tasks.starter: # Even numbers, 2 upwards

tests.why: 7 is odd, so the last line is 6. The counter steps by 2, not by 1.
A 2 gives one line. Nothing at all means the condition stopped before the first turn.
10 is even, so it is displayed too. Use <= and not < in the condition.

hint.think: The counter does not have to go up by 1. What would make it skip the odd numbers?

tasks.q: This program should display 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, one on each line. It never stops. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and watch what happens.
Do not change the number `5` or the condition.
Display 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1, one on each line.
tasks.fb: A loop that runs for ever is the commonest while loop mistake there is, and the cure is always the same: change the variable inside the loop.

tests.why: The loop never stopped, because n stayed at 5 for ever. Add a line inside the loop that makes n smaller.

hint.think: Which of the three parts of a while loop is missing here?
walk: n is set to `5` before the loop.
n is tested in the condition.
Nothing inside the loop ever changes n.

teach.say: A while loop tests the same variable over and over. If nothing inside the loop changes that variable, the condition stays true and the loop runs for ever. The site stops a runaway program after a few seconds. Every programmer writes one sooner or later.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display the line `"Step "`[number] for every number from `1` up to that number.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than `1`.
There is one space after the word Step.
One line of output for each number.
tasks.fb: str() round a number is how it joins onto words, and that has not changed now the number comes from a loop.
tasks.starter: # Step 1, Step 2, and so on

tests.why: Join the word Step to the counter with str( ) round the counter.
One number gives one line.
The counter changes every turn, so each line is different.

hint.think: A number has to be turned into text before it can be joined to a word.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Using a while loop, display every number from it down to `1`, one on each line. Then, using a second while loop, display every number from `1` back up to it, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, which is never less than `1`.
The numbers come down first, then go back up.
The number `1` appears twice, once at the end of the first loop and once at the start of the second.
tasks.fb: Two loops in one program each keep their own count, and the second one has to be set up just as carefully as the first.
tasks.starter: # Down to 1, then back up again

tests.why: Six lines from a 3: three coming down and three going up.
A 1 gives one turn in each loop, so the line appears twice.
The second loop needs its counter set back to 1 before it starts.

hint.think: Two separate loops, one after the other, each with its own counter set up before it.
walk: Read the number.
Count down to `1` in the first loop.
Set a counter back to `1`.
Count up to the number in the second loop.

tasks.q: Press Run. Type 0 and press Enter, then type 12 and press Enter.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
The 0 is refused, so the program asks again.
A loop like this one is called validation.
tasks.fb: Reading once before the loop is what lets a good first answer skip the loop altogether.
tasks.starter:
age = int(input("Age? "))
while age < 1:
    print("Too small")
    age = int(input("Age? "))
print("Thank you")

teach.say: A while loop can keep asking until the answer is allowed. Read one value before the loop. Then, while the value is still wrong, say so and read another.

lines: Read the first value before the loop.
Keep going while the value is still not allowed.
Tell the user what is wrong.
Read another value, which the condition then tests.
This runs once, when the value is finally allowed.

tasks.q: The user types 3, then 7, then 15. What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: Two numbers were refused, so there are two warnings, and only the accepted one is displayed.

tasks.q: Change the program so it keeps asking until the number is `10` or more.
brief: Change only the number in the condition.
A number of exactly `10` is accepted.
Display `"too small"` for each number refused.

n = int(input())
while n < 5:
    print("too small")
    n = int(input())
print(n)

tests.why: A 7 is still being accepted, so the condition still stops at 5.
Exactly 10 is allowed, so the condition uses < and not <=.
A good first number is accepted straight away and nothing is refused.

hint.think: The condition says what counts as wrong, so that is the part to change.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it keeps asking until the mark typed in is `100` or less.

Replace ____ with one instruction of your own.

mark = int(input())
while mark > 100:
    print("too big")
    ____
print(mark)

tests.why: Replace the ____ with an instruction that reads another mark.

teach.say: The second reading goes at the bottom of the loop. Then the condition tests the new value before the loop decides whether to go round again.

tasks.q: Keep asking the user for a whole number until one of them is `1` or more. Display `"Too small"` for every number refused. Then display the accepted number on a line of its own.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until one of them is `1` or more.
A number of exactly `1` is accepted.
Display exactly: Too small
tasks.fb: An if asks once and gives up. A while keeps asking, which is exactly what validation needs.
tasks.starter: # Keep asking until the number reaches 1

tests.why: One number refused gives one warning, then the accepted number.
A good first number is accepted, so the loop runs zero times.
Two numbers refused gives two warnings. One only means an if was used where a while was needed.

hint.think: Read one number before the loop, then keep reading while the number is still wrong.

teach.say: The condition describes what is wrong, not what is right. Here anything below 1 is wrong, so the loop keeps going while the value is below 1.

tasks.q: Keep asking the user for a whole number until one of them is from `1` to `5`. Display `"Out of range"` for every number refused. Then display the accepted number on a line of its own.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until one of them is from `1` to `5`.
Both `1` and `5` are accepted.
Display exactly: Out of range

tasks.starter: # Keep asking until the number is from 1 to 5

1 is the bottom of the range and is allowed, so the condition uses < 1 and not <= 1.
5 is the top of the range and is allowed, so the condition uses > 5 and not >= 5.
6 is just outside the range, which is where < and <= get mixed up.

hint.think: Two ways of being wrong, joined so that either one keeps the loop going.

teach.say: There are two ways of being wrong here, too small and too big, so the two comparisons are joined with or. Either one of them means asking again.

tasks.q: This program should keep asking until the number is `10` or more. It gives up after one go. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and type 3, then 5, then 12.
Display `"too small"` for each number refused.
Then display the accepted number on a line of its own.
tasks.fb: An if and a while look alike and behave very differently: only one of them goes back and checks again.
tasks.starter:
n = int(input())
if n < 10:
    print("too small")
    n = int(input())
print(n)

tests.why: A 5 came out, so the program accepted the second wrong number instead of asking again.
A good first number is accepted either way, so this test passes already.
One number refused looks the same with an if, which is why one test is never enough.

hint.think: An if checks once and then moves on. What checks again and again?

Two words refused gives two warnings.
y is not the word yes, so it is refused. Comparing one letter would let it through.

hint.think: The word is wrong when it is not the first answer and also not the second.

code: c = input()   # the user types pink

Display `"Please type yes or no"` for every word refused. Then display the accepted number. Then display the accepted word on the next line.
brief: The user types in whole numbers first, then words.
Two separate loops, one after the other.
The number is displayed before the word.
Display exactly: Too small, and exactly: Please type yes or no

tasks.starter: # A number to validate, then a word

Both first answers are allowed, so neither loop runs at all.
The number loop must finish before the word loop starts reading.

walk: Read a number and keep asking while it is too small.
Read a word and keep asking while it is neither answer.
Display the number, then the word.

tasks.q: Press Run. Type red, then blue, then `"stop"`.
brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
The word `"stop"` is the signal to finish, so it is not displayed.
A value that means stop is called a sentinel.
tasks.fb: The sentinel is never used, because the condition tests every value before the body gets to it.
tasks.starter:
word = input("Word? ")
while word != "stop":
    print(word)
    word = input("Word? ")
print("Finished")

teach.say: A sentinel is a value that means finish rather than real data. Read one value before the loop. Use it inside the loop. Read the next one at the bottom of the loop, so the condition tests it before it is ever used.

lines: Read the first word before the loop.
Keep going while the word is not the sentinel.
Use the word, because the condition has already let it through.
Read the next word, which the condition then tests.
This runs once, after the sentinel has been typed.

tasks.q: The user types 5, then 8, then 0. What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.
tasks.fb: The 0 is the signal to stop, so it never reaches the print inside the loop.

teach.say: The sentinel is read like any other value, but the condition sends the loop home before the body can display it.

tasks.q: Change the program so the word `"end"` stops the loop instead of the word `"stop"`.
brief: Change only the sentinel in the condition.
Display each word as it is typed, one on each line.
Do not display the word `"end"`.
tasks.fb: Changing the sentinel changes nothing else: the shape of the loop stays exactly the same.
tasks.starter:
word = input()
while word != "stop":
    print(word)
    word = input()

tests.why: The word end came out or the program crashed, so end is not yet the sentinel.
One word before the sentinel gives one line.
Every word before end is displayed, however many there are.

hint.think: The sentinel lives in the condition, inside quotation marks.

tasks.q: Finish the program so it displays each number until `-1` is typed.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type `-1`.
Replace ____ with one instruction of your own.
Display each number as it is typed, one on each line.
Do not display the `-1`.
tasks.fb: Read one before the loop, read the next at the bottom. That pair is the whole pattern.
tasks.starter:
n = int(input())
while n != -1:
    print(n)
    ____

tests.why: Replace the ____ with an instruction that reads the next number.
One number before the sentinel gives one line.
A 0 is ordinary data here and is displayed, because only -1 stops the loop.

hint.think: The loop needs the next number before it tests the condition again.

teach.say: The reading at the bottom of the loop is what lets the next value be tested before it is used. Leave it out and the first value is tested for ever.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type `0`, which means stop. Display each number doubled, one on each line. Do not display anything for the `0`.

At least one number comes before the `0`.
One line of output for each number, which is that number multiplied by `2`.
tasks.fb: The sentinel loop reads, tests, then uses. Nothing is done to a value until the condition has allowed it.

tests.why: Two numbers before the 0 gives two lines, each one doubled.
One number gives one line.
Negative numbers are ordinary data, because only 0 stops the loop.

hint.think: The doubling happens inside the loop, to the value the condition has let through.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type `-1`, which means stop. Add the numbers up. Display the total and nothing else.
brief: The user types in whole numbers, one on each line, until they type `-1`.
The `-1` is not added to the total.
With no numbers at all the total is `0`, and that `0` is still displayed.
tasks.fb: Set it, add to it, display it. A while loop handles a running total exactly as a for loop does.
tasks.starter: # Add the numbers up until -1 stops the loop

tests.why: The three numbers come to 60. A 59 means the -1 was added as well.
No numbers at all, so the total is still 0, and it still has to be displayed.
One number only. Check the total starts at 0 rather than at the first number.
However many numbers there are, the same loop handles them.

hint.think: Three places for the total: set before, added inside, displayed after.

teach.say: A running total works the same here as it did in a for loop. Set it to 0 before the loop, add to it inside the loop, and display it after the loop.

tasks.q: This program should add up the numbers typed before the `-1`. It adds the `-1` as well. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and type 10, then 20, then `-1`.
The `-1` is the signal to stop and is not part of the total.
Display the total and nothing else.
With no numbers at all the total is `0`.
tasks.fb: Reading at the top of the loop lets the sentinel into the body. Reading at the bottom keeps it out.
tasks.starter:
total = 0
n = 0
while n != -1:
    n = int(input())
    total = total + n
print(total)

tests.why: A 29 means the -1 was added. Move the reading to the bottom of the loop.
No numbers at all, so the total is 0. A -1 here means the sentinel was treated as data.
One number only, and the -1 must not change the total.

hint.think: Which values reach the line that adds to the total?
walk: Read one number before the loop.
Add it inside the loop.
Read the next number at the bottom of the loop.

teach.say: The order of the two lines inside the loop decides which values get used. Read at the bottom of the loop, so the condition tests every value before the body touches it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type the word `"end"`, which means stop. Add the numbers up. Display the line `"Total is "`[total].

Read each line as text, and cast it to a number inside the loop.
With no numbers at all the total is `0`.
There is one space after the word is.
tasks.fb: Read as text, test the condition, then cast. Casting too early is what makes a word sentinel crash.

The loop runs zero times. A crash means int( ) was used on the word end.
One number only, and the message still has to be displayed.
int( ) copes with a minus sign, but the line is still read as text first.

tasks.q: Ask the user for whole numbers until they type `-1`, which means stop. Display each number as it is typed, one on each line. Then display the line `"Highest was "`[the largest number]. Display `"none"` instead when `-1` is the very first number typed.

Display exactly: none
There is one space after the word was.
tasks.fb: A largest so far starts at the first value read, never at 0, because the data is allowed to be negative.
tasks.starter: # Show each number, then the largest of them

tests.why: Three numbers, then the largest. A 2 at the end means the last number was displayed rather than the largest.
Nothing was typed, so there is no largest to report.
With one number, that number is the largest.
Both numbers are below 0, so a largest starting at 0 would never be beaten.

hint.think: A largest so far that starts at 0 can never be beaten by a negative number.
walk: Read the first number.
If it is the sentinel, display `"none"`.
Otherwise make it the largest so far, then loop, displaying and comparing.
Then display the Highest was line.

tasks.q: Press Run. Type red, then blue, then `"end"`.

The count is displayed once, after the loop.

Keep going while the word is not the sentinel.

info.title: Stuck forever
info.text: If a program stops responding, an infinite loop is often why: the condition it waits for can never become False.

info.title: Ask again politely
info.text: A good validation loop says what was wrong with the last answer, not just 'try again'.

info.title: Choosing a sentinel
info.text: -1 works when the real values can never be negative. For a temperature it would be a terrible choice.

info.title: Count or total
info.text: A counter always adds 1. A running total adds whatever came in. Plenty of programs need both at once.

info.title: Testing at the bottom
info.text: Some languages have a loop that tests its condition at the end, so it always runs once. Python does not, so the first read goes above the loop.

info.title: No data at all
info.text: A program given no data should still print something sensible. Start every total at zero and it will.
